note.ok: The platform answered this identity normally. Its cookies are accepted and its signature was read.

rotation.title: Rotation
rotation.reservedHint: Out of rotation: only requests that name this identity use it
rotation.mode: What rotation may use it for

modeHint.all: Rotation may hand it to any endpoint. Endpoints that need a login still prefer or require one, and with guests first on, the rest reach a login only when no guest can.
modeHint.limited: Rotation hands it out for the ticked endpoints and nothing else - how a login is kept for the endpoints that need one. A request that names it is never limited by this.
modeHint.reserved: Rotation never hands it out, not even for an endpoint or a later page that needs a login: only a request carrying identity= with its id uses it. It is left out of the pool level.

cookieRoleAbout.required: This build refuses to use an identity without it.
cookieRoleAbout.session: Carries a logged-in session. Far more valuable than a guest jar, and far more damaging to leak.
cookieRoleAbout.useful: Not required, but an identity carrying it is refused less often.
cookieRoleAbout.other: Set by the platform and kept as it was received. Not something this build reads.

cookieAbout.__ac_nonce: A one-time challenge from the anti-crawler layer. Paired with __ac_signature.
cookieAbout.__ac_signature: The answer to the __ac_nonce challenge, computed in the page.
cookieAbout.ak_bmsc: Akamai Bot Manager's session cookie, set by the CDN rather than by TikTok.
cookieAbout.architecture: A hardware hint the page recorded about the browser it ran in. This build sends its own fingerprint values rather than reading these back.
cookieAbout.bd_ticket_guard_client_data: Client attestation data for ByteDance's ticket guard.
cookieAbout.biz_trace_id: A trace id the web app attaches to its own calls.
cookieAbout.bm_sv: Akamai Bot Manager's short-lived validation cookie.
cookieAbout.csrf_session_id: Ties a CSRF token to one session.
cookieAbout.delay_guest_mode_vid: Guest-mode bookkeeping from the web app.
cookieAbout.device_web_cpu_core: How many CPU cores the page saw. A fingerprint hint, not something this build reads back.
cookieAbout.device_web_memory_size: How much memory the page saw. A fingerprint hint, not something this build reads back.
cookieAbout.g_state: State for Google's sign-in widget. Nothing to do with the platform's API.
cookieAbout.IsDouyinActive: Whether the page thought the tab was in the foreground.
cookieAbout.msToken: A short-lived token the page's own JavaScript refreshes. It takes part in request signing; TikTok signing in this build needs it, and requests start coming back empty once it goes stale.
cookieAbout.odin_tt: A long-lived device id. Risk control uses it to tie separate requests back to one device.
cookieAbout.passport_csrf_token: A CSRF token from the account service. Sent back on writes; harmless to read requests.
cookieAbout.s_v_web_id: Douyin's visitor verification id. This build sends it verbatim as both `verifyFp` and `fp`.
cookieAbout.sessionid: A logged-in session. Anyone holding this is signed in as that account.
cookieAbout.sessionid_ss: The secure-only half of the logged-in session.
cookieAbout.sid_guard: The session id with its issue time and lifetime attached; this build reads the expiry out of it.
cookieAbout.sid_tt: Another form of the logged-in session id.
cookieAbout.sid_ucp_v1: A newer wrapper around the logged-in session.
cookieAbout.store-country-code: The region TikTok decided this client is in.
cookieAbout.store-idc: Which datacentre this account's data lives in. Changing it sends requests to the wrong region.
cookieAbout.tiktok_webapp_theme: The site's light-or-dark preference. Nothing to do with requests.
cookieAbout.tiktok_webapp_theme_source: Whether that theme was chosen or inherited from the system.
cookieAbout.tt-target-idc: The datacentre the web app asks to be served by.
cookieAbout.tt_chain_token: Routes a request through the same edge chain as the one before it.
cookieAbout.tt_csrf_token: A CSRF token the web app sends back with its own calls.
cookieAbout.ttwid: ByteDance's device-level visitor id, issued by the CDN edge. Without it a request looks like a client the platform has never seen.
cookieAbout.uid_tt: The account's user id, sent alongside a logged-in session.
cookieAbout.UIFID: A fused device-and-user id. TikTok signing carries it alongside msToken.
cookieAbout.uifid: A fused device-and-user id. TikTok signing carries it alongside msToken.
cookieAbout.UIFID_TEMP: The visitor id a Douyin mint produces, and what the web signature SDK signs with. This build looks for it under six spellings and cannot sign a Douyin request without one of them.
cookieAbout.uifid_temp: The visitor id a Douyin mint produces, and what the web signature SDK signs with.
cookieAbout.UIFIDTEMP: The visitor id a Douyin mint produces, under another of the spellings the SDK accepts.
cookieAbout.uifidtemp: The visitor id a Douyin mint produces, under another of the spellings the SDK accepts.
cookieAbout.buvid3: Bilibili's visitor id, handed to a browser on its first visit. Without it the signed endpoints treat a request as coming from no browser at all.
cookieAbout.buvid4: Bilibili's second visitor id, issued beside buvid3.
cookieAbout.b_nut: When this visitor first arrived on Bilibili, as a Unix time.
cookieAbout.SESSDATA: A logged-in Bilibili session. Anyone holding this is signed in as that account.
cookieAbout.bili_jct: Bilibili's CSRF token for a logged-in session. Only writes need it.
cookieAbout.DedeUserID: The id of the Bilibili account this session is signed in as.
cookieAbout.buvid_fp: A browser fingerprint id the Bilibili page computes and stores.
cookieAbout._uuid: Another Bilibili visitor id the page sets on first load.

groupHint.sched: Waiting, queueing, cooldowns and the thresholds that trip an endpoint.
groupHint.pool: Water marks and the conservative per-identity request rate.
groupHint.signing: Which signer produces the request signature. The in-process algorithms are the default and need no browser; the browser signer is the fallback for the day a platform ships a new SDK.
groupHint.cache: How long a parsed result stays reusable.
groupHint.snapshot: Deduplication window for writes to the content history.
groupHint.retention: How long logs, events and tasks are kept. Content snapshots are never deleted automatically.
groupHint.api: Abuse limits, the long-poll ceiling and the default response language.
groupHint.security: Every key here is sensitive: allowlists, CORS and the download proxy.
groupHint.notify: Delivery switch, channels and the default alert language.
groupHint.system: Instance behaviour, including the daily update check, which is on by default.
groupHint.other: Keys with no group of their own.
groupHint.archive: What this instance keeps after a task result expires. The archive holds the current state of a post; the metric history beside it holds how it changed.
groupHint.capacity: How this instance behaves as the disk fills. It warns, then pauses background writers - it never deletes.
groupHint.media: Where downloaded video and images live, how much disk they may take, and what happens when they reach it. Nothing here is deleted except stored files, and never a pinned one.
groupHint.watchlist: Which targets this instance re-collects on a timer, and how much of the queue that may take. Scheduled runs go through the same queue and identity pool as everything else, so they always yield to a caller who is waiting.

sign.title: Sign a platform API URL
sign.description: Pure arithmetic. Nothing is fetched and no identity is spent.
sign.urlHint: The full API URL including its query. The signature is appended to what you send.
sign.userAgentHint: Douyin and TikTok hash this into the signature; Bilibili's WBI signature does not use it. Leave it blank for a Chrome default.
sign.userAgentPlaceholder: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64) ... Chrome/146.0.0.0 Safari/537.36
sign.msTokenHint: TikTok only. Sealed into the signature, so it must be the token the request will carry - an invented value is worse than none.
sign.msTokenPlaceholder: Leave blank if you have none
sign.checklistTitle: A signature on its own is not enough
sign.checkUserAgent: Send the request with the exact User-Agent the signature was computed for - it is echoed back below.
sign.checkTls: Use a TLS fingerprint that agrees with that User-Agent. TikTok checks, and plain curl is refused whatever the signature says.
sign.checkCookies: Send a cookie jar. A correct signature with no cookies still returns an empty body, because the platform answers a session. Mint one on the next tab.
sign.userAgentEcho: Send the request with this exact string.
sign.cookiesHint: The jar the request will be sent with, in any paste format. Douyin signs over the visitor id inside it, so without one no signature headers are produced.
sign.headersHint: Send every one of these alongside the signed query. Douyin refuses a sign-protected endpoint without them.

stages.title: How this query was assembled
stages.description: One box per layer of the pipeline, in the order the layers ran. A layer that did not run is still shown, with the reason.

reason.no_uifid_cookie: The jar carried no uifid, so Douyin's own signature could not be computed and no signature headers were produced. The sign-protected endpoints will refuse the request naming uifid; mint an identity on the next tab.
reason.no_ms_token_supplied: You supplied no msToken, so an empty one is sent. TikTok accepts a missing token but verifies one that is present, so none was invented.

source.label: msToken source
source.cookies: From the cookie jar you sent
source.generated: Invented here. Douyin accepts a fabricated token; TikTok does not, which is why only Douyin ever shows this.

stages.sealParam: {param} is the parameter that actually seals this request.
stages.inputNotReconstructible: The bytes this layer signed are not always the bytes finally sent, so the input it hashed is not shown - a reconstruction would be right for most queries and silently wrong for the rest.
stages.preimageHint: The signature is the md5 of exactly this string. It was recomputed and checked against the signature before being returned.
stages.preimageUnverified: The preimage did not reproduce this signature when it was checked, so it is not shown: an unverifiable one would be read as documentation of the algorithm.

sign.exampleHint: Fills every field below from a real browser request. The signature parameters are left out because they are what this tool produces, and the cookie values are placeholders - a jar is a live login. Mint a real one on the Identity tab.

decode.title: Read a signature back
decode.description: The inverse of the form beside it. Paste a signed URL and every signature parameter in it is taken apart against the exact string that parameter seals.
decode.valueHint: A whole signed URL is the most useful form: only then is the string each parameter covers known exactly, so only then can the checks run. A single parameter value, or a name=value pair, works too.
decode.userAgentHint: Douyin and TikTok hash the User-Agent into the signature; Bilibili's WBI signature does not. Fill this in and the result says whether the UA you are sending is the one the signature was computed with — which is the most common way a hand-built request fails while looking correct.
decode.parameterHint: Left on auto, the value is identified by properties no other parameter has. Name it yourself if you are holding something unusual.
decode.meaningRecovered: Recovered — in the payload and back exactly: clocks, aid, page_id, the screen the page reported, SDK versions, call counters, nonces.
decode.meaningBound: Bound but not recoverable — the payload carries a hash of the query or the User-Agent, not the thing itself. A hash does not run backwards, so instead of guessing, your candidate is checked against it.
decode.meaningIssued: Not computed at all — msToken and the visitor tokens are issued by the platform or drawn at random. There is no plaintext under them, and saying so is the answer.

source.url: Read out of the URL you pasted, so each parameter was checked against the exact string it seals.
source.parameter: Read as a single parameter. Paste the whole signed URL to check it against the query it was computed over.

checks.title: Inputs checked
checks.covered: The exact {input} this signature was computed over. It reproduced the value above, which is why it is shown.

reason.malformed: This is not a well-formed value of that parameter. The structural test it failed:
reason.one_way: An md5, so there is nothing inside it to recover. What can be done is rebuild the string it covers and confirm it — which is more useful anyway, because that string is what you have to reproduce to sign one yourself.
reason.not_computed: Issued by the platform rather than computed, so there is no plaintext under it. Its shape is still worth checking.
reason.unknown_parameter: This build does not know this parameter.

note.checksum_verified: The internal checksum recomputes. Every input to it is itself a field of the payload, so agreement means the whole layout came back correctly.
note.checksum_disagrees: The internal checksum does not recompute. Either the value was altered in transit or it came from a build of the SDK this one does not match.
note.mixed_verified: The folded timestamp and nonce agree with the fields they were folded from.
note.mixed_disagrees: The folded timestamp and nonce do not agree with the fields beside them.
note.noise_not_recoverable: Some bytes are drawn per call and carry nothing. Two signatures made in the same millisecond differ in most of their bytes and mean the same thing.
note.key_travels_in_the_envelope: The envelope carries its own key — which is how the platform decrypts it, and how this can be read at all.
note.constant_placeholder: TikTok Web sends a literal here on every HTTP request; the real algorithm of this name is only used for websocket handshakes.
note.superseded_by_a_bogus: Douyin has moved on to a_bogus. TikTok Web still accepts this one, and some Douyin endpoints do.
note.issued_by_the_platform: Minted by the platform for a browser. It cannot be computed, only obtained — mint an identity on the identity tab.
note.wbi_keys_unavailable: The key this md5 covers is mixed from two keys Bilibili publishes to every visitor, and this instance could not fetch them just now. The query could not be checked; nothing here says it is wrong.

scheduler.rotationTitle: How one request picks an identity
scheduler.rotationDescription: Five stages, in this order. A request that clears all five gets a lease; anything else is refused with the reason, which is what the request log records.

stage.circuit: The endpoint's circuit. Opened by failures across at least sched.circuit_min_identities distinct identities, so one broken identity cannot close an endpoint for everyone. While open, one probe per interval is let through and everything else is refused without spending anything.
stage.rank: Ranking: health tier first, then least-recently-used, then a per-call jitter. The tier is coarse on purpose - ranking on the exact score makes the single healthiest identity win every time, which is a hot spot rather than a rotation.
stage.inflight: One request at a time per identity. A real session is not parallel, and this is the limit that actually stops one identity absorbing a burst.
stage.quota: A token bucket per identity and endpoint. A list endpoint refills at 0.12/s, so one identity serves roughly one of those every eight seconds however many are queued.
stage.outcome: The result is folded back in: an OK clears the failure streak, a risk-control hit cools the identity for a doubling backoff, and a business error - a deleted video - deliberately changes nothing.

scheduler.fairness: The ordering aims for "no identity is systematically favoured", not for round-robin. Perfect turn-taking needs a global sequencer, because several concurrent callers read the same last-used snapshot before any of them wins a lease.
scheduler.fairnessMeasured: Measured against a uniform random baseline, the resulting spread is no better than chance. What the scheduler does guarantee, and what its tests assert strictly, is exclusivity, quota and that no identity is starved.

mcp.title: MCP
mcp.description: Point an agent at this instance. The same tools, the same identity pool, the same rate limits as the REST API.

endpoint.title: Endpoint
endpoint.body: Generated from the address you reached this page on.
endpoint.authValue: an API key, in an Authorization or X-API-Key header
endpoint.slash: Keep the trailing slash. /mcp answers 307 to /mcp/, and a client that does not re-send the POST on a redirect fails in a way that looks like an auth problem.
endpoint.host: 127.0.0.1 only works for an agent on this machine. An agent somewhere else needs an address it can actually reach, and this instance behind TLS.
endpoint.cookie: The console session cookie is not accepted here. MCP takes API keys and nothing else, so a browser that is already signed in cannot be used as a credential.

mcp.noKeys: There are no API keys yet, and MCP will not accept anything else. Create one under Access control → API keys, with read access to the platforms you want the agent to reach.

configure.title: Client configuration
configure.body: Pick a client. The address is filled in for you; the key is not.
configure.keyNote: Wherever dtk_YOUR_API_KEY appears, put a real key - or, for Codex, set the environment variable the snippet names. A key is shown once when you create it and never again, so if you have lost it, make a new one rather than hunting for the old.

claudeCode.name: Claude Code
claudeCode.where: Run this once. It writes the server into your Claude Code config; add --scope project to commit it to the repository instead.

claudeDesktop.name: Claude Desktop
claudeDesktop.where: claude_desktop_config.json only validates stdio servers, and Claude Desktop's remote-connector screen authenticates with OAuth, which this server does not speak - so this goes through the mcp-remote bridge and needs Node installed. Settings → Developer → Edit Config, merge, restart the app.

codex.name: Codex CLI
codex.where: Append to ~/.codex/config.toml, and export DTK_API_KEY in the shell you start Codex from. Codex reads the key from there so the config file stays safe to commit.

cherry.name: Cherry Studio
cherry.where: Settings → MCP Servers → Add Server → Import from JSON. Cherry Studio calls this transport 'streamableHttp'.

generic.name: Any other client
generic.where: Anything that speaks streamable-http. The request shape it has to make:

stdio.name: stdio (local, no HTTP)
stdio.where: For an agent that spawns the process itself. It talks JSON-RPC over the pipe and reads the same environment as the API, so the two never disagree about which database they are looking at.

tools.title: Tools
tools.body: What the agent can call. Every one of them spends the identity pool exactly as a REST call would.

tool.parse_url: Fetch whatever a link points at. The place to start when you have a URL.
tool.get_video: One post, video or image album, by id.
tool.list_user_posts: An author's posts, one page at a time.
tool.list_comments: Top-level comments on a post, one page at a time.
tool.get_content_history: Recorded metric history for a post or an author.
tool.pool_status: Identity-pool and endpoint health, for when calls start failing.
tool.download_media: Store a post's media on this instance; transcribe_video takes the download_id it returns.
tool.transcribe_video: Transcribe an already downloaded video and return its full text.
tool.get_task_result: Collect a result that did not finish in time.

usage.title: Notes for whoever is writing the prompts
usage.async: Every tool waits for its own answer. When one comes back still running, it returns a task id rather than blocking, and get_task_result collects it - the agent does not need to poll in a loop.
usage.scopes: A key is bounded by the scopes it was minted with, even if an administrator owns it. A key with only douyin:read cannot reach TikTok through MCP any more than through REST.
usage.paging: Listing tools page. Ask for the next page with the cursor they return rather than raising the count, which is the mistake the server instructions specifically warn the agent about.

banner.title: Demo mode.
banner.body: This account is shared, read-only and for trying the project out. Nothing you do here is saved, and the pages that hold credentials are hidden. Deploy your own instance for the full console.

notice.title: A newer release is available
notice.body: This instance runs {current}. The latest release is {latest}.
notice.how: Installed with the install script? Run ./dtkctl upgrade in its directory; it pulls, migrates and restarts, and records the new version itself. Otherwise see "Updating to a new release" in the README. Your data, settings and identity pool are untouched by it.
